procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 23.11.2015 passed by the High Court dismissing the Writ Petition.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a Writ Petition in the High Court challenging the Tribunal's order dated 19.03.2012 (directing the authority not to deport the appellant). The High Court initially stayed the Tribunal's order on 06.06.2012. However, the High Court ultimately dismissed the Writ Petition on 23.11.2015.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order dated 23.11.2015. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, effectively quashing the Tribunal's order dated 19.03.2012 and the High Court's judgment dated 23.11.2015. The Supreme Court also allowed the application for condonation of delay and exemption from filing a certified copy of the impugned judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the report/opinion of the Tribunal dated 16.11.2017, which was sought by the Supreme Court, was sustainable in law.

facts: The Supreme Court, in a previous order dated 28.07.2017, had directed the Foreigners Tribunal to conduct a new inquiry into the appellant's documents and submit a report on their nationality.
The Tribunal complied and submitted a report/opinion on 16.11.2017, which again concluded that the appellant was a foreigner who had entered India illegally after the cut-off date of 25.03.1971.
This report was the central issue for the Supreme Court's consideration.
law: The Supreme Court has the authority to review a report/opinion submitted by a Tribunal at its own request to determine if it is legally sound and sustainable.
application: The Supreme Court conducted a "threadbare" examination of the Tribunal's report/opinion dated 16.11.2017.

Based on this detailed review and for the "totality of reasons afore-indicated" (reasons detailed in parts of the judgment not provided in the text), the Court found the report to be "wholly unsustainable."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Tribunal's report/opinion dated 16.11.2017 was legally unsustainable. As a result, the Court quashed the report. It also proceeded to set aside the Tribunal's original order (dated 19.03.2012) and the High Court's judgment (dated 23.11.2015) that were based on the earlier proceedings.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Tribunal's order dated 19.03.2012 and the High Court's judgment dated 23.11.2015, which declared the appellant a foreigner, were legally valid.

facts: The Foreigners Tribunal, in an ex-parte order dated 19.03.2012, declared the appellant a foreigner because he failed to appear and discharge his burden of proof under Section 9 of the Foreigners Act.
The Gauhati High Court upheld the Tribunal's decision in its judgment dated 23.11.2015.

The appellant had produced evidence showing his parents were residents of an Indian village since 1965, he and his brother were on the 1985 electoral roll, and another sibling had been declared not to be a foreigner by a Tribunal.
The Tribunal had disbelieved the appellant's evidence due to what the Supreme Court later characterized as minor discrepancies in the spelling of names and in dates.
law: Under Section 9 of the Foreigners Act, 1946, the burden of proof lies on the person in question to prove that they are not a foreigner.
The principles of natural justice, specifically 'audi alteram partem' (the right to be heard), obligate authorities to share the material evidence collected against a person with that person.
Authorities cannot initiate proceedings with life-altering consequences based on "hearsay or bald and vague allegation(s)" without providing the underlying material.
application: The Supreme Court found that the authorities violated the principles of natural justice. Although the reference to the Tribunal alleged the appellant was from a specific village in Bangladesh, the authorities never provided the appellant or the Tribunal with the material evidence to support this claim.
The Court held that while Section 9 places the burden of proof on the individual, it does not permit the authorities to bypass their duty to act fairly and share the basis of their allegations.
The Court re-examined the evidence presented by the appellant and determined that the discrepancies in names and dates were "minor in nature" and were not sufficient grounds to disbelieve his claim.

Considering the totality of the evidence—including his parents' residency since 1965, his sibling's citizenship status, and his presence on the 1985 electoral roll—the Court found that the appellant had successfully established his case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the earlier decisions, concluding that they were not legally valid. It found that the Tribunal had wrongly dismissed the appellant's evidence based on minor discrepancies and that the authorities had violated principles of natural justice. Consequently, the Court set aside the orders of the Tribunal and the High Court and declared the appellant to be an Indian citizen.

cases.principle: Provisions imposing a reverse burden of proof must be strictly complied with and may be subject to the proof of some basic facts as envisaged under the statute.

cases.case_name: Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India
cases.principle: Clarifying what is expected of authorities before the statutory burden of proof under Section 9 of the Foreigners Act is triggered.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Provisions imposing a reverse burden of proof must be strictly complied with and are subject to the proof of foundational facts by the party asserting the claim; only after this initial burden is satisfied does the legal burden shift to the person against whom the claim is made. Furthermore, the principles of natural justice must be read into the unoccupied interstices of a statute, unless there is a clear mandate to the contrary, to ensure a fair procedure is followed before a decision affecting rights is made.
obiter: Penal statutes that tend to deprive a person of rights must be given a strict interpretation.
When a fact is especially within the knowledge of any person, the burden of proving that fact is upon them.

If the facts required to form the basis of a presumption of law exist, a court must draw the statutory conclusion, but this does not preclude the person against whom the presumption is drawn from rebutting it.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A grave miscarriage of justice occurred because the State failed to meet its primary onus of setting out the main grounds for the proceeding, which is a prerequisite before the burden of proof can shift to the individual to prove their citizenship. The court found that the principles of natural justice, which require a fair procedure and the opportunity to present a defense, were violated.
legal_tests_applied: A two-step burden of proof framework is applied in foreigner determination cases: First, the State bears the 'primary onus' to set out the main grounds for the proceeding. Only after the Tribunal is satisfied that the State has met this initial burden does the burden of proof shift to the individual (the proceedee) to prove their citizenship, in line with Section 106 of the Evidence Act.

The principles of natural justice must be read into the 'unoccupied interstices of the statute,' meaning that even if a law is silent, there is an inherent requirement to hear the parties whose rights are affected and to follow a fair procedure before making a decision, unless the statute explicitly states otherwise.
policy_considerations: Even if a statute is silent, 'there could be nothing wrong in spelling out the need to hear the parties whose rights and interest are likely to be affected by the orders that may be passed, and making it a requirement to follow a fair procedure before taking a decision, unless the statute provides otherwise.'
'No form or procedure should ever be permitted to exclude the presentation of a litigant’s defence or stand.'

Placing a 'persuasive burden on the accused persons must justify the loss of protection which will be suffered by the accused. Fairness and reasonableness of trial as also maintenance of the individual dignity of the accused must be uppermost in the court’s mind.'
